activities.anchor: Low expansion is the whole trick
activities.caption: pin the thermal-shock survival points on the scale
activities.name: msShockPlace

config.prompt: A surface suddenly cooled cracks when the induced stress reaches σ_f — at ΔT_c ≈ σ_f/(E·α). Soda-lime glass manages about 70 K. Where does borosilicate sit?
config.why: Borosilicate (α ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻⁶) survives ΔT ≈ 240 K where soda-lime (α ≈ 9 × 10⁻⁶) manages about 70 K — which is why ovenware is borosilicate and windows are not; fused silica (α ≈ 0.5 × 10⁻⁶) survives the extreme end.

activities.caption: pair each selection basis with the wire it picks
activities.name: msWireMatch

config.prompt: Same database, different question — pair the basis with its winner:

pairs.right: aluminium — more than twice the current per unit mass

config.why: A selection compares the property combination the objective asks for — the database answers only the question you write down.

activities.caption: derive the index step by step
activities.name: msIndexOrder

config.prompt: From beam theory to the performance index — put the derivation in order:
items: Geometrically similar sections: I scales with A²
Minimising mass means maximising M = E^½/ρ
config.why: Everything except ρ and E is fixed by the specification — and a tension tie gives M = E/ρ, a panel in bending E^⅓/ρ: the exponent encodes the loading geometry.

activities.anchor: evolution optimised trees for exactly this index
activities.caption: file the worked ranking by its numbers
activities.name: msRankBuckets

config.prompt: Worked ranking, (GPa)^½ per (Mg/m³) — file each material by its number:
config.why: The numbers are (GPa)^½ per (Mg/m³); change the objective to cost per unit stiffness and steel surges back — the winner is a property of the question.

activities.anchor: Plot modulus against density for 100,000 materials
activities.caption: pair each class bubble with its address on the chart
activities.name: msBubbleMatch

config.prompt: The point cloud organises into class bubbles — pair class with position:

pairs.right: a diagonal band across the middle

config.why: Slide the guideline across the chart toward the top-left and the first bubble it touches is the winner — an entire ranking performed as geometry, with property envelopes keeping the scatter honest (ceramics' strength spans two decades).

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the shape multiplier
activities.name: msShapeEstimate

config.prompt: How many times the bending stiffness of a solid rod of the same mass does a well-shaped I-beam or box section carry?
config.why: About 10–25 times — so "steel, shaped well" can beat "aluminium, shaped badly"; local instability of thin walls is what sets the ceiling.
config.context: Shape and process are multipliers: process compatibility (castable, weldable, extrudable, printable) and the audit trail of documentation complete the decision.

activities.anchor: Run the whole workflow once, quickly, on a real object
activities.caption: one pass of the method — the bicycle frame
activities.name: msFrameBranch

config.root: One pass of the method, on a showroom object — make the calls.

start.text: A bicycle frame: a set of ties and beams in bending and torsion; objective, minimum mass at acceptable cost. Screening — which candidates die first?

choices.label: Thermoplastics (creep), ceramics (toughness), lead (weight)
choices.feedback: The hard limits do the killing before any ranking begins.

choices.label: Steel, aluminium and titanium — too ordinary
choices.feedback: Those are the survivors — the ranking happens to them, not on them.

choices.label: Whatever fails a price cap only
choices.feedback: A price cap is one constraint among several — decades of fatigue, no rust, joinable, serviceable to −20 °C all bite too.

rank.text: Ranking on E^½/ρ — who tops the list?

choices.label: CFRP, titanium and aluminium, steel below
choices.feedback: Exactly the ranking the index produces — and the showroom confirms it.

choices.label: Steel first — cheapest per tonne
choices.feedback: Cheap is a different objective; on mass-per-stiffness steel sits below the light metals.

market.text: Carbon-fibre racing frames, aluminium mid-range, titanium boutique, steel touring — a translation the buyers made without ever writing it down. Documentation: the layup schedule, the tube supplier's certificate.

config.why: One pass of the method, and the showroom becomes a chart you can read.

activities.anchor: The two indices point in opposite directions
activities.caption: one line of the vessel decision is wrong — find it
activities.name: msVesselSpot

config.prompt: An engineer reasons through a pressure vessel. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: Mass minimisation: maximise σ_y/ρ — the wall as thin as the yield strength allows
Safety: maximise K_IC/σ_y — the vessel must yield before it breaks
Ultra-high-strength steel wins both indices, so it is the choice
The professional answer: a middle-strength, high-toughness steel — or titanium when mass is precious (spacecraft tanks)
config.correction: Ultra-high-strength steel wins the first index and fails the second — its toughness is poor precisely because its strength is high.
config.why: A design with two failure modes needs two indices, and the candidate set is the region where both are satisfied — failure-mode thinking stops the method ranking confidently into catastrophe.
